newsitem.title: USA: Finding funds for young investors.
newsitem.headline: Finding funds for young investors.

text.p: One great way to get your kids off on the right financial foot is to give them a little investment experience while they're still young.
That's why growing numbers of parents are getting their kids involved in investment decisions that affect the children's future.
For example, a child might help choose and monitor the mutual funds that invest his or her college money.

The Stein Roe Young Investor Fund (800-338-2550; $2,500 minimum investment; no-load) was launched in May 1994 to encourage kids' involvement in investing, and it's been a roaring success by any measure.
The number of shareholders (average age: 9 years old) hit 56,000 in December, and assets climbed by 89 percent during 1996 alone, to $323 million.
Kids who invest in the fund get a quarterly newsletter that aims to keep them interested in investing.
The fund promises to invest at least 65 percent of its assets in shares of companies that affect children or teenagers. Thus, it holds shares of household names such as McDonalds and Microsoft.
In fact, however, many of the companies are kid-oriented only in the most indirect way. Co-manager Erik Gustafson has never rejected a stock on the basis that kids wouldn't be interested.
Is the kids' angle just a gimmick? So far, no one cares.
The fund's total return since inception has been an impressive 30.4 percent, compared with 18.6 percent for the average growth fund. Thus, adults as well as kids are throwing cash at it.
So far, the fund hasn't spawned many competitors. But it probably will -- which raises an obvious question: What is a "kid's fund", anyway?
Is it a fund that comes with a newsletter for kids? A fund that calls itself a kid's fund? A fund that promises only to buy stocks that might interest kids?

A better definition might be one along these lines: A kid's fund is one that adopts a solid long-term investment strategy suitable for very young investors. By that definition, a number of different funds qualify.

The Stein Roe entry is among them. It typically holds shares of firms expected to deliver steady earnings growth over time. Those firms are often big domestic blue chips such as Coca-Cola, Gillette and Johnson and Johnson. Such companies' stocks have led the recent surge in stock prices -- accounting for the fund's stellar performance -- and now trade at very high levels.

That said, investment styles change. Sooner or later, the blue chips that the Young Investor Fund favours will stumble. When that occurs, your young investor might want to have some of his or her money in other sectors of the market such as small-company shares or overseas stocks.
No problem, as long as your child doesn't insist on a quarterly newsletter.

Parents who want to get their kids some mutual fund shares should consider entries such as Royce Premier (800-221-4268; $2,000 minimum; no-load), which holds shares of small companies in a variety of industries.

Respected value investor Chuck Royce looks for companies that are leaders in their industries, and invests in the ones he believes are undervalued. He's led the fund to a 14.7 percent annual return since its inception in 1992, with only half as much volatility as the average small-company fund.

Perkins Opportunity (888-737-5677; $2,500 minimum; 4.75 percent load) is another promising small-company fund. Managers Dick Perkins and Dan Perkins favour extremely small companies with strong growth potential due to new products or skilful management. The fund has gained 27.1 percent annually since its inception in 1993.
That said, the small stocks the fund buys can be risky: The fund has been 50 percent more volatile than the average small-company fund during the last three years.

But such shares could provide substantial rewards for young investors who won't draw on their savings for 10 years or more. The fund's 4.75 percent sales charge may deter some investors -- but if a child holds the fund for a decade, the $118.75 charge on a $2,500 investment won't greatly affect his or her returns.

You can further diversify a child's portfolio by buying funds that invest in overseas markets. Such funds typically perform well when U.S. markets are faltering. One solid choice: Managers International Equity (800-835-3879; $2,000 minimum; no-load), which buys shares of large, well-established companies in Europe, Japan, the Pacific Rim and other regions.
During the past five years, the fund's returns have been 88 percent higher than those of the typical foreign stock fund with almost 40 percent less volatility.
(EDITORS: Clint Willis is a freelance writer who covers mutual funds for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Mr. Willis.)
